clinicalPearls: Inflammation is centred on the vitreous, the peripheral retina and the pars plana rather than the anterior segment
The usual symptoms are floaters and blurred vision, typically in a white, comfortable eye with little pain or redness
Vitreous inflammatory aggregates (snowballs) and exudative material over the pars plana (snowbanking) are the hallmark signs, best seen on indented indirect ophthalmoscopy
Cystoid macular oedema is the leading cause of visual loss and should be sought on optical coherence tomography
Recognised associations include multiple sclerosis, sarcoidosis, Lyme disease and tuberculosis, although many cases are idiopathic
Peripheral retinal vasculitis and neovascularisation of the snowbank may occur and can bleed
Treatment follows a stepladder of corticosteroids, then steroid-sparing immunosuppression, with control of macular oedema as the main goal
reference.pathophysiology: Intermediate uveitis is a chronic, predominantly T-cell mediated inflammation of the vitreous base, peripheral retina and pars plana. Inflammatory cells aggregate within the vitreous as snowballs and become organised into a snowbank overlying the inferior pars plana. Breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier and release of inflammatory cytokines lead to cystoid macular oedema, the principal threat to vision. The disorder may be idiopathic or form part of a systemic inflammatory or infective disease such as sarcoidosis, multiple sclerosis or tuberculosis.
additionalInvestigations: Indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral indentation to detect snowballs and snowbanking
Optical coherence tomography of the macula for cystoid macular oedema
Fluorescein angiography to demonstrate peripheral vasculitis and leakage
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain when demyelination is suspected
Serology for Lyme disease and syphilis
Chest imaging and serum angiotensin-converting enzyme for sarcoidosis, with tuberculosis testing
redFlags: Dense vitritis in an older patient, raising the possibility of masquerade lymphoma
Profound or refractory cystoid macular oedema
Vitreous haemorrhage or tractional detachment from snowbank neovascularisation
reference.prognosis: The course is frequently chronic and relapsing; the visual outcome is largely determined by how well cystoid macular oedema is controlled, and many patients maintain good vision with appropriate treatment.
pitfalls: Failing to investigate for an underlying systemic association such as multiple sclerosis or sarcoidosis
Overlooking masquerade lymphoma in older patients with persistent vitritis
Not examining the peripheral retina and pars plana adequately
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course: Uveitis and Ocular Inflammation
